extracted.intended_audience: NPR readers and the general public interested in free speech, media, satire, and censorship
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion/news commentary evaluating media censorship of satire (specifically South Park) and arguing principles for creators, publishers, and institutions about resisting intimidation and protecting free expression. Focuses on how threats and blasphemy taboos shape editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to intimidation
rubrics_metrics.description: Creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone have one thing right that the publishers and networks that censor them don't: resistance to intimidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece endorses creators standing up to threats rather than capitulating; example: Parker and Stone attempted to include Mohammed in the 200th episode despite expected backlash. Implicit evaluation: courage in the face of threats is a positive quality for satirists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let threats dictate editorial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy Central's censorship of a recent South Park episode after threats ... is the latest evidence that the West is slowly surrendering, institution by institution, to diffuse but determined demands to suppress anything possibly deemed as blasphemy against Islam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions (networks, publishers, museums, presses) should avoid letting violent or menacing demands determine what they publish or broadcast. The article cites examples (Comedy Central, Yale University Press, Random House, Metropolitan Museum of Art) where fear led to dropping content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid self-censorship that undermines content
rubrics_metrics.description: For the follow-up 201st episode, Comedy Central ramped up the self-censorship ... this rendered the entire episode 'practically incomprehensible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive bleeping/censorship can make creative works incoherent and defeat their purpose; evaluate censorship decisions against whether they destroy narrative or satirical meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the severity and motive of blasphemy-based threats
rubrics_metrics.description: South Park creators received a death threat not simply for insult but because they had allegedly committed blasphemy against Islam, for which death has been the traditional punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When threats invoke accusations of blasphemy, institutions must understand they are tied to historically severe consequences; this raises real safety considerations but does not, per author, justify capitulation that narrows discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blasphemy rules narrow acceptable discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Abiding by Islamic blasphemy rules is no small matter ... coercively applied blasphemy laws 'narrow the bounds of acceptable discourse ... and prevent most Muslims from thinking "outside the box" not only about religion, but about vast spheres of life, literature, science and culture in general.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article uses Abdurrahman Wahid's observation to argue that enforcing blasphemy taboos limits public debate across many domains; evaluators should weigh long-term harms to free inquiry when judging censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical pattern: extremists target many forms of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Extremists have already reacted violently to statements questioning Islamic doctrine's link to violence (Pope Benedict), protesting the abuse of women (Van Gogh and Hirsi Ali), using the Koran in fiction (Rushdie), ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece lists prior incidents demonstrating that backlash is not limited to a single medium or message; when assessing the risks of publishing controversial satire, consider the broader history of violent reactions to diverse critical works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional capitulation creates a chilling effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of threats to others, Yale University Press, Random House, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and others dropped plans to publish or display ideas and images that touch on Islam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate censorship decisions for their chilling effect: acquiescing to threats signals that extremists can shape public discourse and will likely reduce future publication/exhibition of contentious works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirists have a civic role to challenge taboos
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartoonists, people who do satire -- we're not in the Army, we're never going to be f***ing drafted, and this is our time to stand up and do the right thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames satire as a genre with a responsibility to push boundaries and resist intimidation. As a criterion for producing satire, consider commitment to challenging taboos and defending expressive freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workarounds don't eliminate risk of provocation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the episode, these characters threaten to file a class-action lawsuit ... Mohammed's figure is blacked out, hidden ... and eventually disguised in a goofy mascot-style bear costume. The audience hears him, but never sees his face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics like blacking out images or disguising figures (the 'bear-suit loophole') may be used to avoid direct depiction, but the article notes such strategies can still provoke threats and may be criticized as disingenuous or insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threats can include targeted intimidation tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolution Muslim ... posted a message ... that 'warns' that they 'will probably wind up like Theo van Gogh' ... It also includes Stone and Parker's photos and their production company's addresses ... an audio overlay ... reading a fatwa against blasphemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating safety and editorial decisions, consider that provocations often accompany explicit targeting (naming individuals, posting addresses, graphic imagery, invoking prior murders), which increases real-world danger and ethical dilemmas for publishers.
